post_title: I think I found an angel, and he wants to doc a deal up. I have no idea what I'm doing.
post_body:
I think I found an angel, and he wants to doc a deal up. I have no idea what I'm doing. Basically, I only needed 30k on the project, of which 6k is padding for overruns on the project.  I need the 24k over a three month schedule. 

I was going to doc up a clean LLC, and have the 24k on a note with a draw schedule of 2k/week.  IO at what rate?  12? 20? 4? P-2?  5 year AMORT?  2 year balloon?  

What's the fair way to set this up?  As a note to the LLC?  As a stock ownership deal?  How do I structure payback?  I expect to monetize, or start to monetize within 60 days after the 12 week coding process.  I'm sure I can write the note up like that, with a balloon in a year?  Can I write it into the LLC that I have the option to buy any stock I offer the investor back at a 125% premium?  I have never done a deal like this.

I'm a fish out of water on this deal......Obviously I want it in my favor, but still be equitable for the investor......

I offered 3% ownership for the 30k....maybe I should just stick with that.

Also, I have some IP in the project that I'm personally licensing to the LLC for $1.00.  I wrote it into the operating agreement.

What's the deal with convertible notes, and who does the valuation?  Can it be predetermined that it's 3%?  What's the advantage(s)?
comment:
On the valuation issues thing, I totally agree that a small privately held company would have a real problem coming up with a value.  I don't understand how these convertible note deals come up with a value.  That's a whole other subject that I keep saying I'm going to read up on.
On this deal, the guy literally said, "Send something over to sign."  I have to tell you, for me to get to this point has been harrowing.  I navigated through literally a 100 investors and lenders to get to this.  I come from the collateralized loan side, so this angel/vc was straight up 'idea lending'.  
I've had an interest in a couple LLC's so I'm not foreign to the K-1.  
Funny you said the 125% thing.  I was wondering what the difference was between paying 25% interest or 125%.....Ok, so it's a good idea then to go just with a note.....They get paid first in event of liquidation, right?  Pretty sure it's a better position to be in than member that brings money to the table. I pretend to be a lawyer all the time, so we're cool. So I'll present a note to float and not rock the boat.

Oof, that sounds exhausting. Going through 100 investors/lenders just to finally get a "send something over to sign" would fry anybody's brain.

If I were you, I'd slow this down for one beat and get a startup lawyer + CPA to look at the paper before you float anything. A plain vanilla note can absolutely be cleaner, but only if the terms aren't sneaky. You're close enough to the finish line that it's worth paying for a real review instead of winging it.

post_title: How do you deal with users that hate your company?
post_body:
How do you deal with users that hate your company? I recently joined a tech startup about 6 months ago as a software engineer. I also do some feature and UX design-like stuff. We run a very popular website, one that functions a lot like a dating website and helps you meet new friends and potential partners. We're a big name-- I'm pretty sure some of you would recognize the company and some of you may even be active users. I'd rather leave the name out, as I'm apart of a very small team.

Long story short, we have a lot of users who seem to enjoy protesting our website. Don't get me wrong. We have users who submit legit complaints and we listen to them and take them into consideration as best as we can... But then we have the drama users. Users who enjoy following the hype of how supposedly terrible our website is. We just finished working on a new privacy feature, yet these types of users complain venomously that we're out to get and expose their personal info. They post ""evidence"", not a single bit of which is true. We've had a great track record and nothing really bad has ever happened on our site, yet we have a handful of people still protest saying we're too easy to join and it's too easy to find people to meet up with, so we let in rapists and child molesters. These comments get posted on Twitter and blogged about. These people have sent us hate mail, threatened us with law suites and sometimes even personal threats. They blog about it, write in our discussion forums, and even message new users on the site warning them about how terrible the site is (this is one issue we're currently trying to figure out how to combat).

Yet these users stick around, just like the users who love our site and pay for premium features and speak highly of our community. Yet instead of using our website for the value it gives, they seem to get off on bashing it! Which confuses me!

I guess I'm just trying to figure out the psychology of these types of hateful users. If they hate our site so much, why not to go to a competitor service/community? If we're such terrible people, who do they insist on using our services? I really don't think we're terrible! What's up with these hype-driven haters, and what can we do as a business to put them at ease? We've been thinking about hiring a full time PR person just to focus on dealing with these types of users and the stories people often exaggerate about our community. Do you think this is a good step?
comment: You cannot just go around terminating everyone's account that speaks poorly of your company. Instead focus on the issue from a Marketing perspective. If you are really worried about them effecting your business than you should look at your branding initiatives (the way consumers perceive your company). I am not sure about the exact number of people, but try directly contacting as many of the people who have problems with your site as possible. Could say something like: "Hello, My name is techie443. "The (Company Name) team noticed that you were unhappy with X aspect of our site/company. (Company Name) is devoted to the satisfaction of all our customers and would like to work with you in figuring out any problems." Contacting consumers directly like this will not only suprise them in a positive way, but will open the floor to possible improvements to your site.

That kind of user backlash is honestly draining, especially when you're busting your ass shipping privacy features and people still assume bad intent.

I'd stop thinking about this as "how do we shut them up?" and start treating it like trust repair. A few practical things: 1) publish a plain-English explanation of what the feature does and does *not* do, 2) reply publicly to the biggest misconceptions with screenshots/examples, 3) DM a handful of the loudest reasonable critics and ask for a 15-minute call, and 4) keep a visible changelog so people can see you actually respond to feedback. post_title: How do I monetize my music listings site?
post_body:
How do I monetize my music listings site? I run a website that is a searchable database of live music listings for Key West. The site has over 1,400 pages and gets decent traffic, but has yet to turn a profit. I see it as a labor of love at this point, but hate that it takes a back burner when I get busy with paying ventures.  It brings in about \$20 per month.
Also, I recently started a Facebook page where I post beach, sunrise, sunset and wildlife photos. I push amazon links every other day. I've made \$5 this month. Meh.
I welcome any ideas or advice on how to monetize this thing, beyond what I've already tried.
comment:
A few thoughts on monetization:

The $20/month thing hurts my soul because you clearly have traffic and a dedicated audience. Have you thought about reaching out directly to the bars and venues for sponsored listings or "featured" placement on the calendar? If they're already benefiting from your site driving people through their doors, a $25-50/month featured spot is a no-brainer for them. Even 10 venues paying that and you're looking at real money.

For the Facebook beaches page, affiliate links are a tough game on social media — people just don't click through that way. You might have better luck partnering with local tour operators, snorkel trips, kayak rentals, etc. for a referral commission. That audience is literally in vacation-spending mode.

post_title: Has anyone else had a problem filling entry level technical jobs?
post_body:
Has anyone else had a problem filling entry level technical jobs? We have had an entry level hardware service tech position open for 3 years. I have had 25 applicants over that time period, not one of them has come in dressed in even business casual attire. Most hand in applications/resumes with terrible spelling or grammar issues. Those who did make it through the interview process (service manager, service and sales coordinator, and the general manager) turn down the offer, one because he said to my face he expects (as an entry level tech) to receive at least 50k a year or he'll just keep his unemployment. That clown I turned into the workforce center... 

I started working here 5 years ago making the same wage we're offering the new tech position, and have managed to survive, and actually get completely out of debt. But we can't attract even someone who's been unemployed for 6 months.

comment:
I get why you're frustrated, but three years open is the market waving a giant flag at you. Rural hiring is rough *and* technical people have way more options than they used to.

If you want this role filled, I'd look at four things: raise the pay, rewrite the title so it sounds like a career start instead of a dead-end helper job, add a clear training path/cert reimbursement, and widen the funnel to community colleges/trade schools instead of just waiting for random applicants. You can also split the role: hire for attitude/basic competence and train the hardware-specific stuff in-house. Entry-level candidates will absolutely tolerate lower experience requirements before they'll tolerate below-market pay.

post_title: A 5% angel investor is trying to steal my $4M startup through endless fraudulent lawsuits. We're running out of money. What are my options?
post_body:
Hello, reddit!

We are one start-up focusing on healthcare IT with a market valuation of $4M. I am the sole founder and CEO. We have been in operation since Oct, 2012. We were doing great winning many awards and got good funding support.

Everything was fine until late last year we got an angel investor on board with an investment of $200K. He only had 5% of the company and yet was sitting on the board of the company. I am the sole founder of the company and has one seat on the board. There are 3 seats on the board in the operating agreement. But whenever I proposed the 3rd board member, he always vetoed it and said that the 3rd seat was to be saved for later (the operating agreement says that the founder has the right to propose candidates but the preferred share holder/this investor has to approve it).

During the 4th month since his investment, he asked me to hand over all company documents and he would like to have his people in charge of company finances and he also would like to get $250K as annual salaries. As the founder and CEO and Chairman of the board, my salary was $60K then. I did not agree as I sensed that he had exterior motives to seize control of the company. After we did not agree with each other, he filed petition to dissolve the company and he sets up a company as the receiver of the company. He also used his personal connection to work with Howard Bank to freeze our company bank account (which I fought hard to get our money back), and coerced our payroll company to add him as the new system admin (which I discovered and had him removed within the same day), and also sent numerous emails to harass company employees, telling them not to speak with me at all as I am fired by him and he is the new self-appointed CEO. He also reached out to our company key officers and tried to buy them to get them recognize him as the new CEO. He also acted like the new CEO and called for company meeting but no one from my company responded to the meeting. He was in rage, and called all other company creditors and members, claiming that he is the new CEO and I am fired. He also called our company landlord, asking them to change company office lock so that I can not enter to ""threaten company properties"". Several of our young employees got really confused by his emails and after getting his threatening phone calls, they all went home and refused to return to work. One employee with heart diseases immediately fell ill and got a fever and could not work any longer with us.

post_title: So my partner says 'We need to have a serious chat'.
post_body:
So my partner says 'We need to have a serious chat'

So last night my partner and I were driving home last night and we got into an argument about money. It's tough sometimes in this game because you don't know when you're going to be getting paid or whether your business is going to take off. 
  
My partner has been very supportive of me and my life goals to try and get my business off the ground but then disaster had struck and I was forced to shutdown my call centre of 7 operators overnight. Lost, I tried to re-enter the workforce but found I was not employable. 
  
Not to be swayed, I researched more and more and started building new relationships and a new business off the ground which is starting to show some return. However I had forgotten one main thing: my partner. 
  
My partner supported my efforts but it's been a year now and my partner's now tired and sick of it and just wants a normal life and I sympathize with that. There was no luxuries or expensive dinners, no holidays or getaways. My partner sat me down and told me that we should end it.
comment: Sorry it came down to that for you, it is a good reminder to balance life and business. Best of luck my friend.

Yeah... that's a scary sentence to hear, but honestly it might be the conversation you two have needed for a while.

I'd go into it ready to listen, not defend. Ask what "normal life" actually means to your partner in concrete terms: income floor, timeline, hours, stress, family time, savings, whatever. If your partner has carried this for a year, they probably need evidence that there's a shared plan now, not just more hope.

post_title: Does anyone else just feel overwhelmed by all there is to read, learn, and do? And how do you handle it?
post_body:
Does anyone else just feel overwhelmed by all there is to read, learn, and do? And how do you handle it? I'm in perhaps one of my most UNemcumbered times of my life right now. No kids, no boyfriend, cheap rent, not many friends locally - so that all adds up to a lot of time by myself. I'm working a part time job plus trying to kick my freelancing into a higher gear, write creatively, and lose weight by going to the gym 3x a week minimum. 
 
I also want to stay on top of things going on in the world, learn from others, read articles from thought-leaders and those professionals I admire or the people who write about them. I'm trying to stay on top of trends in my industry... and if I did all that, I'd have no time for anything else. I constantly feel like I'm 10 steps behind. I haven't watched movies lately (and as an aspiring screenwriter, that's BAD) I'm barely getting any reading time, and yet I'm busy from the moment I crack my eyes open until I can finally switch my brain off at the end of the day. I have trouble falling asleep but I'm constantly tired...  
 
The things I *should* be doing, like writing pitches for magazines/websites and trying to get a staff writing job are falling by the wayside. I can't cut out the workouts either, without them my mental health deteriorates pretty quickly and the bike rides to and from the gym are really enjoyable. 
 
I'm listening to podcasts on my 2x/wk commute to try and maximise my time.... but honestly. How do you all balance everything? How can I start? My life is in disarray!
comment: I feel like this is exactly my problem! I've been feeling 'so busy' with everything, but when I look back on what I've accomplished during the day, I realise I've been spending all my time on the 'fun' stuff and less important stuff and leaving the important things ie. paperwork pile up. Might have to check the book out!

post_title: I love being a business owner! I just hate it so much.
post_body:
I love being a business owner! I just hate it so much.
RANT INCOMING!

I shouldn't complain. I really shouldn't. Things are going alright, we're in the black, and my job isn't thankless; more than many can say. I like what I do, and I like what I've done. I get a joy out of it that is great.

I don't mind the very long hours. 
I don't mind the stress of needing to perform to make rent.
I don't mind that nine or so people rely on me for their daily bread, or that my decisions will make or ruin me.

I also feel abit of resentment towards me that I'm not working a regular 9-5 it's disheartening.
comment:
Nevermind the haters and keep pushing. When I tell people that I am "working on my own stuff" or that "I am working from home on my business" they often reply with "Oh, so you don't have a job..."

Most people aren't made for freedom, they aren't made to achieve greater things in life and they are incredibly scared of the unknown as well as success. Yes, people are scared of success and the successful people.

So keep on pushing and doing what makes you happy.

post_title: Why is it so hard to be healthy while working a demanding job?!
post_body:
Why is it so hard to be healthy while working a demanding job?! Is this a struggle for anyone else?
I have been working a pretty demanding job for the past 5 years. I know I should eat well and exercise because health is so important but it always seems as if work gets in the way. I will go through phases where I will plan, grocery shop, eat really well, exercise, etc. for a couple weeks but then something at work comes up that seems more important to focus on at the time and boom! My healthy efforts go out the window until I decide I need to be healthy again. It is so frustrating.
comment: Consider meal prepping to save time during busy days. This can help you maintain a healthy routine.

comment:
This is such a common trap, so don't beat yourself up over it. A demanding job will happily eat every bit of structure you don't protect.

What usually works better is lowering the friction instead of waiting for motivation: 2-3 default breakfasts, prepped lunches, groceries on autopilot, workouts short enough that you won't skip them, and some kind of "minimum viable health" plan for crazy weeks. Even a 20-minute walk + basic meal routine is infinitely better than the all-or-nothing cycle.

post_title: The downsides of entrepreneurship.
post_body:
The downsides of entrepreneurship.
I feel guilty doing anything that doesn't directly or indirectly grow my business. A lot of my past hobbies have faded away. A lot of the people I hung out with are barely considered friends anymore. I don't spend money of fun things for myself. It takes a toll on you and the people close to you.

I'm getting out of entrepreneurship for a while. Maybe I'll come back to it. But for now, I want my life back.
comment: Yeah, some people just stay in business mode all the time. For a lot of founders that never really turns off.

comment:
Honestly, this is a really self-aware post, and a lot of people don't admit it until they're completely fried. Wanting your life back is not quitting at life — it's noticing the cost got too high.

If you're stepping away, I'd make it deliberate. Set work hours again, reconnect with one or two hobbies even if they feel rusty, see friends without turning every conversation into business, and give yourself a decompression window before deciding what's next. If you do come back later, you'll probably build with much better boundaries.
